To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
declining atmospheric deposition of heavy metal pollutants over the last three to four decades is reflected in the soil and foliage of old-growth beoch stands in the Vienna woods.
soil and foliar chemistry of beech stands in Vienna Woods has improved significantly since the implementation of heavy metal emission controls.

the mean soil contents of the heavy metals Pb, Cu, Ni, Mn, Fe and Zn in the stemflow and between tree area decreased significantly within the last three decade and that the foliar contents of the heavy metal Pb, Cu, Mn, Zn, Fe and Ni decreased significantly.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the long-term effects of declining heavy metal deposition on the soil-plant system of beech stands.
the effects of declining atmospheric deposition on heavy metal contents of soils and foliage of beech trees.
the long-term effects of atmospheric deposition on soil and foliar heavy metal contents of beech trees.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the implementation of emission control measures in Austria has led to a significant decline of heavy metal pollution in beech stands of the Vienna Woods.
declining deposition of atmospheric pollutants is reflected in the soil and foliage of beech stands in a complex way.
the heavy metal pollution of the Vienna Woods is declining and has become less critical for the beech stands.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Vienna Woods is an example of a forest ecosystem recovering from heavy metal pollution, which is in line with the general trend of declining heavy metal deposition in Europe.
the Vienna Woods are still heavily influenced by heavy metals, but that their impact is decreasing.
the Vienna Woods is a success story of environmental policy.

long-term changes of soil and foliar heavy metal concentrations are detectable in forest ecosystems.
